title: Is a settled town settled for good?
hook: Cheapest-first settles each town for good. This map has one road that gives money back.

knows: a road has a cost, added along a route
doesNotKnow: that a settled label is only final when no road has negative cost
that checking every road repeatedly makes no such assumption

misconception: Dijkstra's cheapest-first rule always finds the cheapest route.
objective: The learner can explain that cheapest-first locks a town on the assumption that no later road can make it cheaper, that a negative road breaks this (here A locks at 2 though 1 is possible, and C inherits the error: 4, not 3), and that checking every road repeatedly (Bellman-Ford) does not rely on it.

claims.text: With roads S to A 2, S to B 3, B to A -2 and A to C 2, the cheapest cost to A is 1 (S, B, A: 3 - 2) and to C is 3.
claims.source: Builder's node script (Bellman-Ford to a fixed point, 2026-10-14): A = 1, B = 3, C = 3. By hand: S-B-A-C = 3 - 2 + 2 = 3. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Own node Bellman-Ford to fixed point (fc9): A 1, B 3, C 3; by hand S-B-A = 3-2 = 1, S-B-A-C = 3.

claims.text: Cheapest-first with settled labels final locks A at 2 (the cheapest unsettled label when A is settled), and when B is settled later the road B to A offers 1, which is ignored.
claims.source: Builder's node trace of the settle-once version: settle S (A 2, B 3), settle A (label 2; C 4), settle B (B to A offers 3 - 2 = 1, A is settled, ignored). Final A 2, B 3, C 4. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Own node settle-once trace, matching Demo.tsx tapTown(): settle S (A 2, B 3), A (C 4), B offers A 1 to a settled town, ignored (stage 'too late'); final A 2, B 3, C 4.

claims.text: Checking roads in the order #1 S to A, #2 A to C, #3 S to B, #4 B to A, pass 1 prices C at 4 from the old A (2) before road #4 fixes A to 1, so C is still 4 after pass 1; pass 2 re-checks road #2 and lowers C to 3. Every town priced from a wrong label inherits the error.
claims.source: Demo.tsx v3 runPass() over PASS_ORDER [S>A, A>C, S>B, B>A]. Hand trace: pass 1 from {S 0}: S>A A=2; A>C C=4; S>B B=3; B>A 3−2=1<2 so A=1 → {A 1, B 3, C 4}; pass 2: A>C 1+2=3<4 so C=3 → {A 1, B 3, C 3}; pass 3 unchanged. The general point (an under-relaxed label propagates until its out-edges are relaxed again) is the Bellman-Ford path-relaxation property, CLRS 3rd ed. §24.1 and Lemma 24.15. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own trace of v3 runPass over PASS_ORDER [S>A, A>C, S>B, B>A]: pass 1 A 2, C 4, B 3, then A 1; pass 2 C 3; pass 3 no change. Reveal text matches.

claims.text: Checking every road in the numbered order S to A, A to C, S to B, B to A: after pass 1 the labels are A 1, B 3, C 4; after pass 2 they are A 1, B 3, C 3.
claims.source: Demo.tsx v3 runPass() over PASS_ORDER; hand trace in c3. Road order is a design choice shown on the stage (#1 to #4 tags; the pass highlights the roads that changed a label). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Same trace: after pass 1 {A 1, B 3, C 4}, after pass 2 {A 1, B 3, C 3}.

claims.text: Settling a town assumes no later road can make it cheaper; a road with negative cost breaks that assumption, and Dijkstra's algorithm is proven correct only for non-negative edge weights.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 22.3 (Dijkstra's algorithm assumes non-negative weights; 3rd ed. 24.3). · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: CLRS 4e section 22.3 states Dijkstra for nonnegative edge weights and proves correctness (Theorem 22.6) under that assumption (3e 24.3, Thm 24.6); counterexample c1-c2 shows the failure. Book not re-opened this pass; section numbering confirmed against 4e chapter layout (ch. 22 Single-Source Shortest Paths). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Settled-label failure shown by c1-c2; the Dijkstra correctness proof needs non-negative weights. CLRS 4e 22.3 / Thm 22.6 (3e 24.3 / Thm 24.6) from my knowledge, not opened this pass; the sentence rests on the counterexample and the standard proof.

claims.text: Bellman-Ford keeps no locks, re-checks every road, and costs more checks than cheapest-first (n - 1 passes over all roads).
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 22.1 (Bellman-Ford, |V| - 1 passes; handles negative weights and detects negative cycles); Bellman 1958, Quart. Appl. Math. 16. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: CLRS 4e 22.1: BELLMAN-FORD makes |V|-1 passes relaxing every edge, O(VE), vs Dijkstra O((V+E) lg V) with a binary heap; here 3 x 4 = 12 relaxations vs 4. Bellman 1958, 'On a routing problem', Quart. Appl. Math. 16(1): 87-90 (citation details recalled, not opened).

recall.question: Why can cheapest-first (Dijkstra) give a wrong cost when one road has a negative cost?
options: It locks a town assuming no later road can make it cheaper, and a negative road can
It never looks at roads leaving a town with a negative label
It checks every road too many times
recall.why: Locking a town is only safe if costs never fall along a route. A refund road can cut a locked town's cost after the lock, and every town priced from it inherits the error.
